trans-unit.target: "Baskets" lists every order a customer validated, whether the payment went through or not.
"Promotional codes" holds the codes the shop writes and hands out, with what each takes off and how many times it can still be spent.
"Gift cards" lists the cards sold or issued by hand, their remaining balance and the order that issued them.
Once the order is handled, declare the row dealt with rather than running the whole check again: it leaves the default view and comes back on its own if the problem reappears.

The check is read. None of this raises anything of its own: an order charged and never delivered has no error page and no e-mail to report itself. This screen is the only place it shows, and it only serves if it is opened.
Open the list of orders: a count does not say what to do, whereas the unfolded list names the orders behind it, each with its link to open it in the back office. That is where the work starts.

The panel takes you to the health check, which gathers everything the site verifies on its own. Six of those rows are about your orders: a payment taken whose order never went out, an order delivered with no payment answering for it, an amount or a currency that does not match, an order delivered without its invoice number, lines that do not add up, a basket holding an article withdrawn from the catalog.

Find the order rows: they carry the basket-integrity kind and each says how many orders it found. Orders placed in test mode are left out, otherwise a shop rehearsing its checkout would read every one of them as a defect.
Run the check again. The six checks run on their own every week; this button runs them straight away, if the page is empty or if you have just fixed something.
Choose the code itself, what the customer types in their basket. It is dictated and retyped: keep it short and free of anything read two ways.
Choose the kind, percentage or fixed amount. This choice is what the next field is read by, the two sharing one column.
Bound what it may do: how many orders may spend it at most, the minimum an order has to reach, and the two dates framing it. Each one refuses the code on its own, at the moment the order is frozen.

The code is live. Its counter is raised by settled orders alone, and its test mode column says which mode the shop was charging in the day it was written: a rehearsal code is never spendable for real.
Add a code with the usual button. Unlike a gift card, a code holds no money and is written straight into the form.
The panel takes you to the promotional codes. Every one the shop wrote is listed there, with what it takes off and how often it has been spent.
Set what it takes off. The value is read as a percentage for the first kind, and in cents for the second: ten is either a tenth of the order or ten cents off it.
Check that it is in place: the tile is no longer highlighted and now offers to turn it off. That is the only sign to read, the sending itself only showing on the next order.
Place a rehearsal order in test mode: its confirmation should arrive with the files ticked on that template. If none comes, the switch is on but nothing was ticked in the e-mail builder.

Turn the sending on. The tile stays highlighted while it is off: handing the customer the terms they accepted as a file, rather than as a link to a page rewritten afterwards, is what the law calls a durable medium.

The panel takes you to the dashboard, where the shop's switches sit as tiles. This one decides whether your order e-mails carry files at all; which files is ticked template by template in the e-mail builder.
Set the amount. It is typed in the shop's own currency and becomes the card's whole balance, which its holder spends over as many orders as it takes.
Copy the code down: it is shown once, in the message above the listing you land back on. No screen prints it again, so hand it over before leaving that page.
Mint the card. The code is drawn at random on submit, the same way a purchase draws one: nothing about it is typed.
The panel takes you to the gift cards. All of them are listed there, sold or issued by hand: the ones written here are told apart by naming no order.
Open the issuing form with the button above the listing. There is no new button: the balance is minted from the amount rather than typed, and never edited afterwards.
Set an end date, or none. Left empty, the card never expires; filled in, it stops being spendable that day, whatever balance is left on it.
Set the amount. It is typed in the shop's own currency and VAT included, as every price here is; the tax is taken out of it at the rate the setting holds.
Write the order. It is frozen there and then, and its short address appears above the form: send it by text message or by e-mail, and it is settled online like any other.
Give the customer's address: the confirmation goes there once the order is settled, and it is what attaches the order to their account should they open one.
Name what is being charged for. It is what the customer reads on their order, on their invoice and in their confirmation e-mail: "deposit for the flooring", "bicycle repair".
The panel takes you to the baskets: a payment link is written from the orders listing, which is where the one it creates comes to sit.
Open the form with the button above the listing. There is no row to start from: the order is written by the form it opens.
The round is closed: a marked order leaves the ones awaiting shipping, so tomorrow's sheet will hold only what is still owed.
Narrow to the paid orders: it is the only state a parcel leaves on. An order merely validated has not been settled, and nothing is posted for it.
Put the zone in service: only an active zone is read at checkout. Save, then write the next zone the same way.

Have the grid checked: the health check screen reports what it does not say, no zone at all, no default zone or several of them, a zone without a boundless tier. Read it once the grid is written, rather than on a month of orders.
Pick the countries posted at this tariff. Leave the list empty for the default zone, the one a country named nowhere else falls into: write that one too, or such an order is delivered free of charge.
Name the zone. The name is yours alone: "France", "European Union", "Rest of the world". The customer never reads it.
Add a zone. A zone groups the countries you post at one tariff, and carries its weight tiers with it.
The panel takes you to the shipping zones, which list the ones already written. An empty list is a shop posting everything free of charge.
Write the weight tiers, one price per tier, the parcel charged at the first it fits in. End with a tier left without a ceiling, otherwise a parcel heavier than any of them is posted free of charge.
Print the labels: one sheet for the whole round, opened in another tab. It gathers the orders awaiting shipping that carry an address, and says so when there are none.
The panel takes you to the baskets. Every order is listed there, whatever its state, which is more than a shipping round needs.

Mark one order sent, on the row of the one you have just packed. The button only shows on a paid order carrying something to post and not yet marked; the click records the shipping and e-mails the customer.
Check the customer side: the basket shows its test-payment banner. Run a full payment to check the order does turn into paid.
Disable the test mode with the same shortcut, its label now changed: the shop switches back to the real keys.
Real payments resume. The test payment stays among the payments, told apart by an order carrying no invoice: a rehearsal never enters the invoice sequence.
Enable the test mode: the shop switches to the active provider's test keys, and nobody is charged while it stays on.
The panel takes you to the dashboard: the test-payments shortcut sits there, next to the maintenance one.
Trace the full order: the basket column leads back to the baskets screen, carrying the address, the content and the order's status.
Open a payment's detail: the originating basket, the currency and the transaction id are gathered there.
The panel takes you to the payments: each is listed there with its provider, its amount and its status.

Check the transaction at the provider: the icon opens it on Stripe's dashboard, once an id has been recorded. Revolut publishes no stable address for an order, so the icon is absent there and only the id is shown.
"Payments" lists what has been taken in, with the reference of the transaction at the provider.
"Shipping zones" groups the countries posted at one tariff, each with its weight tiers.
